title: Convex sets, polyhedra and extreme points

blocks.text: 1.2.3 Convex Sets, Polyhedra and Extreme Points

GridCap's maintenance manager has to split part of the 2028 money between two programs: distribution maintenance ($`d`$, in $k) and vegetation management ($`v`$, in $k). Unlike the projects of lesson 1.2.1, these are amounts, not yes/no choices: any value between the limits will do. There are infinitely many allowed splits, so the brute force of lesson 1.1.1 cannot list them. Yet the best one can be found by checking five points. This lesson shows why: what shape the allowed splits form, where on that shape the best split must lie, and why the yes/no decisions of earlier lessons lose that shape. Five rules, one per heading.
The numbers below are round on purpose; GridCap is a fictional utility and this is a teaching example on it, not any real utility's data.
Each Linear Row Cuts Space in Half, and the Rows Together Make a Polyhedron
The manager's rules, written as rows of $`Ax \le b`$ (lesson 1.2.1), with the plan $`(d, v)`$:

items: **crews:** $`d + 2v \le 4000`$, crew-days, since a $k of vegetation work takes two crew-days and a $k of distribution work one;
**veg_cap:** $`v \le 1500`$, only so many miles of line need clearing;
**dist_floor:** $`d \ge 500`$, a commitment to the regulator, written $`-d \le -500`$;

blocks.text: The objective is risk removed, 2 points per $k on distribution and 3 per $k on vegetation: maximize $`2d + 3v`$.

A = np.array([[1, 1],      # d +  v <= 3000   (budget)
              [1, 2],      # d + 2v <= 4000   (crew-days)
              [0, 1],      #       v <= 1500  (vegetation cap)
              [-1, 0],     # -d     <= -500   (distribution floor: d >= 500)
              [0, -1]])    #      -v <= 0     (v >= 0)
b = np.array([3000, 4000, 1500, -500, 0])
c = np.array([2, 3])       # risk points removed per $k

(d, v) = (2000, 1000): feasible True, breaks []
(d, v) = (2500, 1000): feasible False, breaks ['budget', 'crews']
(d, v) = (400, 200): feasible False, breaks ['dist_floor']

The plan has two variables, $`d`$ and $`v`$, so each plan is a point in a plane: two **dimensions**, one per variable. A model with $`n`$ variables has its points in $`n`$ dimensions, one coordinate per variable, and "$`n`$ dimensions" in this lesson always means "$`n`$ variables".

Picture one row on a chart with $`d`$ across and $`v`$ up. The points where $`d + v = 3000`$ form a straight line, and the line splits the plane in two: on one side $`d + v < 3000`$, on the other $`d + v > 3000`$. The row keeps one side and the line itself. That kept side is a **half-space** (in two dimensions, a half-plane).

Every row keeps a half-space, and a feasible point must be in all of them at once. The set of points that satisfy every row of $`Ax \le b`$ is therefore an intersection of half-spaces, which is what a **polyhedron** is:
\{\, x : Ax \le b \,\} = \bigcap_{r} \{\, x : a_r^\top x \le b_r \,\}
In two dimensions a bounded polyhedron is a polygon. Here it has five straight edges, one per row, because each of these five rows bounds it somewhere.
A Polyhedron Is Convex: The Segment Between Two Feasible Points Stays Feasible

Take two feasible splits, $`p = (500, 0)`$ and $`q = (1000, 1500)`$, and walk the straight segment between them. Each point on it is $`(1 - \lambda)\,p + \lambda\, q`$ for a $`\lambda`$ between 0 and 1: $`\lambda = 0`$ is $`p`$, $`\lambda = 1`$ is $`q`$, and $`\lambda = 0.5`$ is the midpoint. Such a point is a **convex combination** of $`p`$ and $`q`$.

It is a special case of a wider idea. A **linear combination** of vectors $`p`$ and $`q`$ is $`\alpha\, p + \beta\, q`$ for *any* two numbers $`\alpha`$ and $`\beta`$, negative or larger than 1 included; with more vectors, each gets its own number. A convex combination is the linear combination whose numbers are not negative and add up to 1, here $`\alpha = 1 - \lambda`$ and $`\beta = \lambda`$. Linear combinations reach the whole plane; convex combinations of two points reach only the segment between them.

p, q = np.array([500, 0]), np.array([1000, 1500])
print("segment from", tuple(p.tolist()), "to", tuple(q.tolist()))
for lam in (0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1):
    point = (1 - lam) * p + lam * q
    print(f"  lambda {lam:<4}: {tuple(point.tolist())} feasible {is_feasible(point)}")

segment from (500, 0) to (1000, 1500)
  lambda 0   : (500, 0) feasible True
  lambda 0.25: (625.0, 375.0) feasible True
  lambda 0.5 : (750.0, 750.0) feasible True
  lambda 0.75: (875.0, 1125.0) feasible True
  lambda 1   : (1000, 1500) feasible True

A set is **convex** when this always happens: for any two of its points, the whole segment between them is in the set. Five sample points are not a proof, but the proof is two lines. If $`Ap \le b`$ and $`Aq \le b`$, and $`0 \le \lambda \le 1`$, then
A\big((1-\lambda)p + \lambda q\big) = (1-\lambda)\,Ap + \lambda\,Aq \;\le\; (1-\lambda)\,b + \lambda\, b = b

The first step is how matrix products distribute; the inequality holds because $`1 - \lambda`$ and $`\lambda`$ are not negative, so multiplying by them keeps each $`\le`$ the right way round. So **every** polyhedron is convex, whatever $`A`$ and $`b`$ are.
Why care? Because in a convex set there are no hidden pockets: if a point is better than where you stand, the straight path towards it stays feasible. Section 2's algorithms rely on this.
Extreme Points Are Where Two Rows Are Tight at Once

An **extreme point** (or **vertex**) of a polyhedron is a feasible point that is not the midpoint of any segment between two other feasible points: a corner. In two dimensions a corner is where two edges meet, so two rows are **tight** there (met with equality, lesson 1.2.1) and their lines cross.

That gives a recipe. For each pair of rows, solve the two equations $`a_i^\top x = b_i`$ and $`a_k^\top x = b_k`$ together. If the rows are parallel there is no single crossing point. If the crossing breaks some other row, it lies outside the polygon. Otherwise it is a vertex.

for i, k in itertools.combinations(range(len(b)), 2):
    pair = A[[i, k]]
    if abs(np.linalg.det(pair)) < 1e-12:
        found.append((names[i], names[k], None, "parallel"))
        continue
    point = np.linalg.solve(pair, b[[i, k]]) + 0.0   # both rows hold with equality; + 0.0 turns -0 into 0
    found.append((names[i], names[k], point, "vertex" if is_feasible(point) else "outside"))

`np.linalg.solve` solves the 2-by-2 system. `np.linalg.det` is the **determinant** of the pair. For a 2-by-2 matrix with rows $`(p, q)`$ and $`(r, s)`$ it is the number $`ps - qr`$. It is 0 exactly when one row is a multiple of the other, so the two lines are parallel and do not cross at a single point, and then there is nothing to solve:

for i, k in ((0, 1), (2, 4)):
    (p, q), (r, s) = A[[i, k]]
    print(f"det {names[i]} & {names[k]}: {p}*{s} - {q}*{r} = {p * s - q * r},"
          f" np.linalg.det gives {np.linalg.det(A[[i, k]]):.1f}")

det budget & crews: 1*2 - 1*1 = 1, np.linalg.det gives 1.0
det veg_cap & veg_nonneg: 0*-1 - 1*0 = 0, np.linalg.det gives 0.0

The budget and crews rows, $`(1, 1)`$ and $`(1, 2)`$, cross at one point. The rows of `veg_cap`, $`(0, 1)`$, and `veg_nonneg`, $`(0, -1)`$, are multiples of each other ($`-1`$ times), so their determinant is 0. The loop over all ten pairs prints:

budget & crews      vertex   (d, v) = (2000, 1000)    objective 7,000
    budget & veg_cap    outside  (d, v) = (1500, 1500)
    budget & dist_floor outside  (d, v) = (500, 2500)
    budget & veg_nonneg vertex   (d, v) = (3000, 0)       objective 6,000
     crews & veg_cap    vertex   (d, v) = (1000, 1500)    objective 6,500
     crews & dist_floor outside  (d, v) = (500, 1750)
     crews & veg_nonneg outside  (d, v) = (4000, 0)
   veg_cap & dist_floor vertex   (d, v) = (500, 1500)     objective 5,500
   veg_cap & veg_nonneg parallel
dist_floor & veg_nonneg vertex   (d, v) = (500, 0)        objective 1,000
5 vertices; best (d, v) = (2000, 1000), objective 7,000
Ten pairs, five vertices. `budget & veg_cap` crosses at (1500, 1500), which needs 4,500 crew-days, so it lies outside. `veg_cap` and `veg_nonneg` are both "v equals a number": parallel lines.

In $`n`$ dimensions the rule is the same with $`n`$ in place of two: a feasible point is a vertex when, among the rows tight there, $`n`$ are **linearly independent**, meaning none of those $`n`$ rows is a linear combination of the others, so together they pin down a single point. The **rank** of a set of rows is the largest number of them that are linearly independent, and NumPy's `np.linalg.matrix_rank` computes it:

rows = np.array([[1, 0],
                 [0, 1],
                 [1, 1]])
combo = 1 * rows[0] + 1 * rows[1]            # a linear combination of rows 0 and 1
print("1*(1, 0) + 1*(0, 1) =", tuple(combo.tolist()), " equals row 2:", bool(np.all(combo == rows[2])))
print("rank of (1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1):", np.linalg.matrix_rank(rows))
print("rank of (1, 0), (0, 1):        ", np.linalg.matrix_rank(rows[:2]))
print("rank of (1, 1), (2, 2):        ", np.linalg.matrix_rank(np.array([[1, 1], [2, 2]])))

The three rows have rank 2, not 3: $`(1, 1)`$ is $`(1, 0) + (0, 1)`$, so it adds no new direction. Any two of them are independent. $`(1, 1)`$ and $`(2, 2)`$ have rank 1, because the second is twice the first: the same line, the zero-determinant case above.
To test a point, keep only its tight rows. A boolean mask (lesson 1.2.1) picks rows out of a matrix: `A[mask]` is the rows where the mask is `True`.

for point in (np.array([2000, 1000]), np.array([1000, 500])):
    tight = np.abs(A @ point - b) <= 1e-9        # a boolean mask, one entry per row
    T = A[tight]                                 # only the rows where the mask is True
    print(f"(d, v) = {tuple(point.tolist())}: tight {[n for n, t in zip(names, tight) if t]},"
          f" A[tight] has shape {T.shape}, rank {np.linalg.matrix_rank(T)}")

(d, v) = (2000, 1000): tight ['budget', 'crews'], A[tight] has shape (2, 2), rank 2
(d, v) = (1000, 500): tight [], A[tight] has shape (0, 2), rank 0

At (2000, 1000) two rows are tight and their rank is 2, the number of variables: a vertex. At (1000, 500), inside the polygon, no row is tight. `A[tight]` is then an empty matrix, 0 rows by 2 columns, and `matrix_rank` returns 0 for it, fewer than 2: not a vertex.
<!-- practice 1 -->
A Linear Objective Is Best at an Extreme Point

The best vertex removes 7,000 risk points. Could a split that is not a corner do better? Search a grid of 496 splits, every $100k in each direction, and then ask GLOP, OR-Tools' linear programming solver (lesson 1.1.3):

grid: 496 points, 281 feasible, best objective 7,000 at [(2000, 1000)]
GLOP: OPTIMAL, (d, v) = (2000, 1000), objective 7,000

Both land on the vertex `budget & crews`. That is not luck. The points where $`2d + 3v`$ takes one value form a straight line, and raising the value slides that line, parallel to itself, across the polygon. The last point it touches before leaving is a corner, or a whole edge if the objective is parallel to one, and an edge ends in corners. Written as a rule: **if a linear program over a polyhedron with at least one vertex has an optimum, some vertex is optimal.** So with the vertices in hand, the best one is a single `max`:
best = max(vertices, key=lambda p: c @ p)

The OR-Tools documentation makes the same point with its first LP example ("Solving an LP Problem"), which finds the optimum by sliding the objective line across the feasible region until it last touches it. Adapted here to MathOpt, with every vertex listed beside GLOP's answer:

def solve_with_glop() -> tuple[str, float, float, float]:
    model = mathopt.Model(name="lp-example")
    x = model.add_variable(lb=0, name="x")
    y = model.add_variable(lb=0, name="y")
    model.add_linear_constraint(x + 2 * y <= 14, name="c1")
    model.add_linear_constraint(3 * x - y >= 0, name="c2")
    model.add_linear_constraint(x - y <= 2, name="c3")
    model.maximize(3 * x + 4 * y)
    result = mathopt.solve(model, mathopt.SolverType.GLOP)
    return (result.termination.reason.name, result.objective_value(),
            result.variable_values(x), result.variable_values(y))

GLOP: OPTIMAL, (x, y) = (6.0, 4.0), objective 34.0
  vertex (x, y) = (2, 6)  objective 30  tight ['c1', 'c2']
  vertex (x, y) = (6, 4)  objective 34  tight ['c1', 'c3']
  vertex (x, y) = (0, 0)  objective  0  tight ['c2', 'x_nonneg', 'y_nonneg']
  vertex (x, y) = (2, 0)  objective  6  tight ['c3', 'y_nonneg']

GLOP's answer is the best of the four vertices, (6, 4), where c1 and c3 are tight. Note the `>=` row: MathOpt takes it as written, and only the vertex search flips it into $`-3x + y \le 0`$. The corner (0, 0) has three tight rows in two dimensions; any two of them are independent, so it is a vertex all the same, and the search reaches it from three different pairs (the program lists it once).

This is the idea the simplex method of lesson 2.2.2 is built on: it walks from vertex to vertex, each time to a better neighbour, instead of trying every pair of rows, which grows fast with the number of rows and variables.
<!-- practice 2 -->
Yes/No Decisions Break Convexity, and That Is Why Integer Programming Is Hard
Return to the tiny GridCap projects of lesson 1.2.1, where each $`x_j`$ is 0 or 1. Take two of its 8 feasible plans and their midpoint:

plans = X[:, feasible]
p, q = plans[:, 1], plans[:, 2]
mid = (p + q) / 2

plan p : [0 1 0 0 0 0 0 1]
plan q : [0 1 0 0 0 0 1 0]
middle : [0.  1.  0.  0.  0.  0.  0.5 0.5]
middle satisfies A x <= b: True
middle is a plan (all 0 or 1): False

The midpoint satisfies every row, as convexity promises, and it funds half of P007 and half of P008, which is not a plan. The set of allowed plans is a scattering of separate points inside the polyhedron, and a set of separate points is not convex.

That breaks the shortcut of the previous section. Drop the 0/1 requirement, let each $`x_j`$ be anything from 0 to 1 (the **LP relaxation** of lesson 1.1.3), and GLOP finds the best vertex of the polyhedron:

It funds 0.655 of P006 and 0.345 of P007, and claims $2,039.0k against the $1,396k of the best real plan (lesson 1.2.1). Every allowed plan is itself a corner of this polyhedron, since each of its $`x_j`$ sits on a bound, 0 or 1. But the polyhedron has other corners too, fractional ones, and here the best corner is one of those. So "the best is at a vertex" finds the best fractional point, not the best plan. Rounding the fractions is no fix either; section 3 shows why, and what solvers do instead.
The Model
The two-variable split this lesson solved, complete.
**Sets.** $`K = \{d, v\}`$, the two programs (distribution maintenance, vegetation management).

**Parameters** (round teaching numbers on fictional GridCap). Budget 3,000 ($k); crew-days 4,000, with 1 crew-day per $k of distribution and 2 per $k of vegetation; vegetation cap 1,500 ($k); distribution floor 500 ($k); risk points removed per $k, 2 for distribution and 3 for vegetation.
**Variables.** $`d \ge 0`$ and $`v \ge 0`$, continuous, in $k.
**Objective.**
\max \; 2d + 3v
**Constraints.**
Its feasible set is a polygon with five vertices, and its optimum is the vertex $`(d, v) = (2000, 1000)`$, where budget and crews are both tight, with objective 7,000.
Summary

items: **Each linear row keeps a half-space, and the rows together make a polyhedron**, the set $`\{x : Ax \le b\}`$.
**A polyhedron is convex.** The segment between two feasible points stays feasible, for any $`A`$ and $`b`$.
**Extreme points are where enough rows are tight at once**: two in two dimensions, $`n`$ linearly independent ones in $`n`$.
**A linear objective is best at an extreme point.** GLOP and a grid search both agree with the best of the five vertices.
**Yes/no decisions break convexity.** The midpoint of two plans is not a plan, and the LP relaxation's best vertex can be fractional.

blocks.text: Reference

rows: The points on one side of a line (plane), and the line itself
The points satisfying every row of $`Ax \le b`$
Contains the segment between any two of its points
A row met with equality, slack 0
A feasible point that is no midpoint of two other feasible points
No row is a linear combination of the others
The largest number of linearly independent rows
The model with each 0/1 variable allowed anywhere in [0, 1]
Determinant, $`ps - qr`$ for rows $`(p, q)`$, $`(r, s)`$: 0 when its rows are dependent
Number of linearly independent rows of `M`; 0 for a matrix with no rows
The rows of `A` where the boolean `mask` is `True`

blocks.text: **Further reading:** [Solving an LP Problem (OR-Tools)](https://developers.google.com/optimization/lp/lp_example) (the example adapted above, with the feasible region drawn and the objective line slid to the optimal corner); [MathOpt sample linear_programming.py](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/math_opt/samples/python/linear_programming.py) (a three-variable LP solved with GLOP, reading the status before the values); [Solving a MIP Problem (OR-Tools)](https://developers.google.com/optimization/mip/mip_example) (an LP relaxation whose best corner is fractional and far from the integer optimum); [NumPy `matrix_rank`](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.linalg.matrix_rank.html) (how NumPy computes rank, from singular values and a tolerance); [NumPy `linalg.solve`](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.linalg.solve.html) (solving a square system, and the error a singular one raises).
Challenges

items: Change the objective to $`3d + 3v`$. It is now parallel to the budget row. Which points are optimal, and are any of them vertices?
Add the row $`d \le 2500`$. How many vertices does the polygon have now, and does the optimum move?
A rule says vegetation gets either nothing or at least $800k. Draw the allowed values of $`v`$ on a line. Is that set convex?

blocks.text: Design Note: Enumerating Vertices Is a Lesson, Not a Method

Trying every pair of rows works for five rows in two dimensions. With $`m`$ rows and $`n`$ variables the number of candidate corners is "$`m`$ choose $`n`$", which for a model of a few hundred rows and variables is far beyond counting. The point of this lesson is the geometry, not the enumeration: it tells you where an LP's optimum lives, and why the 0/1 models of section 3 need more than an LP solver.
The Full Programs

Each snippet above is part of a complete program, and each program printed the output the lesson shows. Open one to read it whole, change it, and run it again: Run starts the program on your copy of the code, so the course's own files never change.

**polygon.py.** The two-program split as $`A`$, $`b`$ and $`c`$; checks three points and walks a segment between two feasible ones (*Each Linear Row Cuts Space in Half* and *A Polyhedron Is Convex*). *Try:* Walk the segment from (500, 0) to (2000, 1000) instead. Predict whether every point is feasible before you run it.

**vertices.py.** Solves every pair of rows and sorts the results into parallel, outside and vertex (*Extreme Points Are Where Two Rows Are Tight at Once*). *Try:* Change the crews limit to 3,500. Which pairs change kind?

**independence.py.** A linear combination, the rank of three rows, two determinants worked by hand, and the tight rows at a vertex and at an inside point picked with a mask (*Extreme Points Are Where Two Rows Are Tight at Once*). *Try:* Add the row `[2, 0]` to `rows`. Predict the rank before you run it.

**grid_vs_vertex.py.** A grid search and a GLOP solve of the same split (*A Linear Objective Is Best at an Extreme Point*). *Try:* Change `c` to `[3, 3]` and predict how many grid points tie for best.

**lp_example.py.** Adapted from the OR-Tools example "Solving an LP Problem": the same LP solved with GLOP through MathOpt, and every vertex of its feasible region with the rows tight there (*A Linear Objective Is Best at an Extreme Point*). *Try:* Change the objective to $`x + 2y`$, parallel to c1, in both `c` and `model.maximize`. Predict which vertices tie for best, and which one GLOP returns.

**not_convex.py.** The midpoint of two tiny GridCap plans, and the LP relaxation of the lesson 1.2.1 model (*Yes/No Decisions Break Convexity*). *Try:* Take the midpoint of `plans[:, 0]` and `plans[:, 7]` instead. Is it a plan?
